questions.en: …the existence of a graph Cay(p) of diameter 3 is equivalent to the existence of a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n; see [2]–[4]. The latter is an important problem in geometry, and its non-existence is a famous conjecture in geometry.

Frobenius (sharply flag-transitive) case of Kantor's theorem on flag-transitive projective planes

questions.formal_statement: Setting printed in the article: n > 8 is an integer such that p = n² + n + 1 is prime. [ASSUMPTION: standard definitions supplied] A projective plane of order n has n²+n+1 points and n²+n+1 lines. Each line is incident with n+1 points and each point with n+1 lines. Any two distinct points lie on exactly one common line, and any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point. The plane is Desarguesian if it is isomorphic to PG(2,q) over a finite field F_q (then n = q). It is flag-transitive if some group of collineations is transitive on its flags (incident point–line pairs). Conjecture (the article says 'its non-existence is a famous conjecture in geometry'): for no such n does a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n exist. Citing [2]–[4], the article links this to the non-existence of a diameter-3 graph Cay(p); as printed, that Cayley-graph wording is defective (see q4). [ASSUMPTION — supplied general form, using Kantor [3] as cited: a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive plane of order n forces p = n²+n+1 to be prime and a Frobenius group of order p(n+1) to act sharply flag-transitively. Every projective plane of order ≤ 8 is Desarguesian, so the printed conjecture is equivalent to 'every finite flag-transitive projective plane is Desarguesian'.] [ASSUMPTION — supplied number-theoretic form, NOT printed in the article: equivalently, for every n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime, the subgroup D = {x ∈ F_p^* : x^{n+1} = 1} (|D| = n+1) is not a planar (p, n+1, 1) difference set in (Z_p, +). That is, the n(n+1) = p − 1 differences d − d′ (d ≠ d′ in D) do not cover all nonzero residues mod p. For n = 2 and n = 8 this D is a planar difference set, giving PG(2,2) and PG(2,8); this fits the article's restriction n > 8.]
questions.solved_means: Either a proof that for every n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime there is no non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n, or a counterexample. By the supplied reformulations, a proof is the same as showing that every finite flag-transitive projective plane is Desarguesian, or that μ_{n+1} ⊂ F_p^* is never a planar difference set mod p for such n. A counterexample would be an explicit non-Desarguesian flag-transitive plane, e.g. an n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime for which μ_{n+1} is a planar difference set mod p. Ruling out ranges or congruence classes of n is only partial progress.

questions.formal_statement: [ASSUMPTION: standard definitions supplied] For a finite group G and subgroups X, Y ≤ G, 'G = XY' means G = {xy : x ∈ X, y ∈ Y}, equivalently |G| = |X||Y|/|X∩Y|. A subgroup H ≤ G is core-free if core_G(H) = ⋂_{g∈G} g^{-1}Hg = 1. Problem 1 (research programme): study the finite groups G that have a factorization G = XY with either (①) X and Y both core-free in G, or (②) X in some special class 𝒞 of groups and Y core-free in G. [ASSUMPTION: 'study' is read as classify or describe the structure.] [ASSUMPTION: the article does not specify 𝒞; natural instances from its Cayley-graph motivation are cyclic, abelian, dihedral, metacyclic, nilpotent or solvable groups.] Motivation printed in the article: if A = Aut Cay(G,S), then A = GH with H a vertex stabilizer, so A is factorizable and the regular subgroup G is a factor. [supplied: H is core-free in A because A acts faithfully.]
questions.solved_means: This is an open-ended programme. A full answer would be an explicit classification of the finite groups with a core-free factorization G = XY, and of those with X in a prescribed class 𝒞 and Y core-free. For example, it could list all triples (G, X, Y) up to conjugacy or automorphism, typically by reducing to almost simple groups. Classifications for particular classes 𝒞 (e.g. cyclic or abelian X) would be partial progress.

questions.formal_statement: Let Γ be a finite, connected, undirected graph [ASSUMPTION: also of valency ≥ 3, the setting of the Tutte–Weiss theorem]. [ASSUMPTION: standard definitions supplied] An s-arc is a sequence (v_0, …, v_s) of vertices with v_{i−1} ~ v_i for 1 ≤ i ≤ s and v_{i−1} ≠ v_{i+1} for 1 ≤ i ≤ s−1. Γ is s-arc-transitive if Aut Γ is transitive on its s-arcs; the article's wording is 'all arcs of length s are equivalent'. The article cites the Tutte–Weiss theorem: s ≤ 7. A Cayley graph Cay(G,S) is defined for S = S^{-1} ⊆ G [ASSUMPTION: 1 ∉ S]: its vertex set is G, and x ~ y iff y ∈ Sx. It is connected iff ⟨S⟩ = G. Problem 2: characterize (classify) the s-arc-transitive Cayley graphs, in particular those with s > 1 (s ≥ 2) and the Cayley graphs Cay(G,S) of groups G in special classes. [ASSUMPTION: the classes are not specified in the article; examples are abelian, cyclic, dihedral, metacyclic, nilpotent or simple groups.]
questions.solved_means: This is open-ended. A full answer would be an explicit classification of the connected s-arc-transitive Cayley graphs with s ≥ 2. One form is a reduction theorem showing that all such graphs are normal covers of an explicitly determined list of basic graphs, together with that list. Another is a complete classification for each specified class of groups, e.g. all 2-arc-transitive Cayley graphs of dihedral or abelian groups.

questions.en: Finally, let G be the dihedral group of order 2p, where p = n² + n + 1 is a prime. Assume n > 8, let S be a set consisting of n+1 conjugate involutions in G, and let Cay(p) = Cay(G, S). Then the diameter of Cay(p) is at most 3, and the existence of a graph Cay(p) of diameter 3 is equivalent to the existence of a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n (see [2]–[4]). … Therefore we propose Problem 3: Prove that for all primes p = n² + n + 1 with n > 8, the diameter of the graph Cay(p) equals 2.

questions.formal_statement: Literal statement. For every integer n > 8 with p = n² + n + 1 prime, let G = D_{2p} = ⟨a, b | a^p = b² = 1, bab = a^{-1}⟩. Let S ⊂ G be a set of n+1 conjugate involutions, and let Cay(p) = Cay(G, S), with vertex set G and x ~ y iff y ∈ Sx. Claim to be proved: diam Cay(p) = 2. Since p is odd, the involutions of D_{2p} are exactly the p reflections ba^i, and they are all conjugate. The article does not say which n+1 of them form S. Printed premises: (A) diam Cay(p) ≤ 3; (B) a diameter-3 Cay(p) exists iff a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n exists; (C) the non-existence of such planes is a famous conjecture. Problem 3 is presented as following ('因此') from these. DISCLOSED INCONSISTENCY (not repaired): every s ∈ S is a reflection, so s·x is a reflection when x is a rotation and a rotation when x is a reflection. Hence Cay(p) is bipartite, with parts ⟨a⟩ and G∖⟨a⟩ (p vertices each), and has valency n+1 < p. The identity is adjacent only to the n+1 elements of S. For each of the remaining n² reflections r, the distance d(1, r) is odd and > 1, hence ≥ 3. So diam Cay(p) ≥ 3 for every admissible n and every choice of S, and the literal claim is false in every instance. Premise (A) also fails in general. Let D_S = {i ∈ Z_p : ba^i ∈ S}. Distinct rotations a^j, a^k are at distance 2 iff k − j ∈ D_S − D_S. Since |D_S|(|D_S| − 1) = p − 1, diam Cay(p) = 3 iff D_S is a planar (p, n+1, 1) difference set; otherwise diam Cay(p) ≥ 4 (or ∞). Premise (B) depends on S and fails for arbitrary S. Example: n = 17 gives p = 307, which is prime, and a Singer difference set of the Desarguesian plane PG(2,17) yields a diameter-3 Cay(p). [ASSUMPTION: choice of S not printed] Premise (B) holds, via Kantor [3], for S0 = {ba^d : d ∈ D} with D = {x ∈ F_p^* : x^{n+1} = 1}, up to automorphisms of G. [ASSUMPTION — nearest internally consistent Cayley-graph reading, NOT printed: 'for all such n, diam Cay(G, S0) ≠ 3, i.e. ≥ 4'. This is equivalent to the geometric conjecture q3 and is recorded only as disclosure, not as a separate question.]
questions.solved_means: As printed, a solution would be a proof that diam Cay(p) = 2 for all primes p = n²+n+1 with n > 8. No such proof can exist. The bipartiteness argument above shows diam Cay(p) ≥ 3 for every admissible n and S, so the literal statement is refuted outright. This follows from the article's own definitions, not from the literature. The open question the article intends is q3. Under the flagged reading 'diam Cay(G, S0) ≠ 3 for all such n', solving it is exactly solving q3.

output.summary: Li Caiheng's short article introduces Cayley graphs, links their automorphism groups (A = GH) to factorizations of finite groups, and poses two open-ended research programmes: Problem 1 on factorizations G = XY with core-free factors (or with X in a special class), and Problem 2 on characterizing s-arc-transitive Cayley graphs, especially for s > 1 and special group classes. questions.best_known: Does every finite flag-transitive projective plane have to be Desarguesian? This remains unresolved in the sources checked through 2026-10-15. The largest explicit plane-order exclusion located is n<200000000000 in Thas–Zagier [0]; Xia [1] supplies later necessary conditions. No later range extension or viable full-resolution claim was located, which is a dated search finding rather than a proof of openness.
questions.gap: The unbounded nonexistence problem remains: exclude every n>8 with p=n²+n+1 prime for which μ_(n+1) is a planar difference set, or construct and verify a counterexample. Necessary conditions and finite exclusions do not settle that question. The reduction is credited to Kantor and Thas–Zagier, independently of the defective printed graph formulation.

questions.best_known: Resolved negatively as printed. Every generator is a reflection, so edges switch the rotation and reflection cosets. Both parts have p vertices, while degree n+1<p; an unjoined opposite-part vertex cannot be reached in two steps, proving diameter at least 3. Li [4], Example 4.5, additionally gives a published counterexample family: the incidence graph of PG(2,17) is an admissible dihedral Cayley graph with p=307 and diameter 3. Thus unspecified reflection sets also invalidate the claimed equivalence with non-Desarguesian planes. The printed upper bound 3 fails too: for S={ba^i:0≤i≤17}, the exponent difference set has only 35 residues, leaving rotations at distance greater than 2.
questions.gap: No gap remains in refuting diameter two. For an exponent set E of size n+1, diameter 3 is equivalent to E being a planar difference set, by counting the p−1 ordered nonzero differences. Restricting E to μ_(n+1) and asking that diameter differ from 3 recovers q3, but those changes are not printed in the book.

identified_counterpart.formal_statement: Setting printed in the article: n > 8 is an integer such that p = n² + n + 1 is prime. [ASSUMPTION: standard definitions supplied] A projective plane of order n has n²+n+1 points and n²+n+1 lines. Each line is incident with n+1 points and each point with n+1 lines. Any two distinct points lie on exactly one common line, and any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point. The plane is Desarguesian if it is isomorphic to PG(2,q) over a finite field F_q (then n = q). It is flag-transitive if some group of collineations is transitive on its flags (incident point–line pairs). Conjecture (the article says 'its non-existence is a famous conjecture in geometry'): for no such n does a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n exist. Citing [2]–[4], the article links this to the non-existence of a diameter-3 graph Cay(p); as printed, that Cayley-graph wording is defective (see q4). [ASSUMPTION — supplied general form, using Kantor [3] as cited: a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive plane of order n forces p = n²+n+1 to be prime and a Frobenius group of order p(n+1) to act sharply flag-transitively. Every projective plane of order ≤ 8 is Desarguesian, so the printed conjecture is equivalent to 'every finite flag-transitive projective plane is Desarguesian'.] [ASSUMPTION — supplied number-theoretic form, NOT printed in the article: equivalently, for every n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime, the subgroup D = {x ∈ F_p^* : x^{n+1} = 1} (|D| = n+1) is not a planar (p, n+1, 1) difference set in (Z_p, +). That is, the n(n+1) = p − 1 differences d − d′ (d ≠ d′ in D) do not cover all nonzero residues mod p. For n = 2 and n = 8 this D is a planar difference set, giving PG(2,2) and PG(2,8); this fits the article's restriction n > 8.]
identified_counterpart.solved_means: Either a proof that for every n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime there is no non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n, or a counterexample. By the supplied reformulations, a proof is the same as showing that every finite flag-transitive projective plane is Desarguesian, or that μ_{n+1} ⊂ F_p^* is never a planar difference set mod p for such n. A counterexample would be an explicit non-Desarguesian flag-transitive plane, e.g. an n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime for which μ_{n+1} is a planar difference set mod p. Ruling out ranges or congruence classes of n is only partial progress.

questions.formal_statement: Does every finite flag-transitive projective plane have to be Desarguesian? Equivalently, for n>8 with p=n^2+n+1 prime, show D={x in F_p*: x^(n+1)=1} is not a planar difference set.
questions.relation_to_book: The geometric nonexistence conjecture is explicitly stated in the article. Its literal diameter-two Cayley-graph assertion is inconsistent; disclose it rather than silently correcting it.

identified_counterpart.formal_statement: Setting printed in the article: n > 8 is an integer such that p = n² + n + 1 is prime. [ASSUMPTION: standard definitions supplied] A projective plane of order n has n²+n+1 points and n²+n+1 lines. Each line is incident with n+1 points and each point with n+1 lines. Any two distinct points lie on exactly one common line, and any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point. The plane is Desarguesian if it is isomorphic to PG(2,q) over a finite field F_q (then n = q). It is flag-transitive if some group of collineations is transitive on its flags (incident point–line pairs). Conjecture (the article says 'its non-existence is a famous conjecture in geometry'): for no such n does a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n exist. Citing [2]–[4], the article links this to the non-existence of a diameter-3 graph Cay(p); as printed, that Cayley-graph wording is defective (see q4). [ASSUMPTION — supplied general form, using Kantor [3] as cited: a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive plane of order n forces p = n²+n+1 to be prime and a Frobenius group of order p(n+1) to act sharply flag-transitively. Every projective plane of order ≤ 8 is Desarguesian, so the printed conjecture is equivalent to 'every finite flag-transitive projective plane is Desarguesian'.] [ASSUMPTION — supplied number-theoretic form, NOT printed in the article: equivalently, for every n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime, the subgroup D = {x ∈ F_p^* : x^{n+1} = 1} (|D| = n+1) is not a planar (p, n+1, 1) difference set in (Z_p, +). That is, the n(n+1) = p − 1 differences d − d′ (d ≠ d′ in D) do not cover all nonzero residues mod p. For n = 2 and n = 8 this D is a planar difference set, giving PG(2,2) and PG(2,8); this fits the article's restriction n > 8.]
identified_counterpart.solved_means: Either a proof that for every n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime there is no non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n, or a counterexample. By the supplied reformulations, a proof is the same as showing that every finite flag-transitive projective plane is Desarguesian, or that μ_{n+1} ⊂ F_p^* is never a planar difference set mod p for such n. A counterexample would be an explicit non-Desarguesian flag-transitive plane, e.g. an n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime for which μ_{n+1} is a planar difference set mod p. Ruling out ranges or congruence classes of n is only partial progress.

sources.citation: Cai Heng Li, [Finite s-arc transitive Cayley graphs and flag-transitive projective planes](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228757029_Finite_s-arc_transitive_Cayley_graphs_and_flag-transitive_projective_planes), Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 133 (2005), 31–41, DOI 10.1090/S0002-9939-04-07549-5.
sources.finding: Example 4.5 supplies Cayley realizations of classical projective-plane incidence graphs using Singer groups and a duality. At n=17, p=307, this gives an admissible reflection-generated dihedral Cayley graph of degree 18 and diameter 3: a counterexample to literal q4. The paper's separate Γ(q) construction specifies an automorphism orbit; it does not justify the book's arbitrary-S equivalence or diameter-two assertion. The valid q3 reduction used here comes from Kantor plus Thas–Zagier.

sources.citation: Binzhou Xia, [Cyclotomic difference sets in finite fields](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.03275), Mathematics of Computation 87 (2018), 2461–2482, DOI 10.1090/mcom/3311.
sources.finding: Develops character-sum and polynomial criteria for cyclotomic and modified cyclotomic difference sets, including nonexistence for even indices through 22 other than 2,4,8. Section 5.3 explicitly connects planar difference sets to q3 and retains the conjecture. Its characteristic-two classification does not settle q3, whose ambient field F_p has odd prime order.

sources.citation: Koji Momihara, Qi Wang and Qing Xiang, [Cyclotomy, difference sets, sequences with low correlation, strongly regular graphs, and related geometric substructures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1809.03007), in Combinatorics and Finite Fields (2019), 173–198.
sources.finding: The survey's Section 2.1 and Theorem 2.6 connect q3 to the broader cyclotomic difference-set classification conjectures. It retains these conjectures and discusses the computational exclusion. It also warns that Feit's power-of-two exclusion and Ott's prime-power-order argument contain errors; their combination is not an accepted solution.

sources.citation: Pingzhi Yuan and Hu Yahui, [A note on power residue difference sets](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/256735294_A_note_on_power_residue_difference_sets), Journal of Algebra 291 (2005), 269–273, DOI 10.1016/j.jalgebra.2004.09.029.
sources.finding: Identifies a gap invalidating the proofs of Ott's principal power-residue and sharply flag-transitive-plane conclusions. This is primary evidence against treating the older apparent resolution as established; it does not itself resolve q3.

owner_selection.relation_to_book: The geometric nonexistence conjecture is explicitly stated in the article. Its literal diameter-two Cayley-graph assertion is inconsistent; disclose it rather than silently correcting it.
owner_selection.baseline: Thas-Zagier, JEMS10(2008): no non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane for order n<200000000000. No later range extension located in the dated screen.
owner_selection.bounded_target: Try to extend the computed nonexistence range to at least n<2000000000000, with exact interval coverage, known-case controls, a survivor/elimination table, and independent checks. Any finite range is a sub-question only.
owner_selection.angle: Harden the staged segmented prime-divisor sieve plus 128-bit Montgomery base-two test on n=8 mod24. Restrict sieve rejection to proper divisors q<p. Controls must reproduce the published exceptional list. Declare the imported Feit/congruence theorems.
owner_selection.risk: High plausibility for a producing range extension is inference, not a promise of proof. Sampled Python pow cross-checks and hashes do not certify every tested n; report that limit explicitly. Do not attack the trivial false literal diameter claim. Probable-prime survivors remain unresolved, not eliminated.
review_requirements: Do not say the target is the book Cayley-graph form or follows from the book stated equivalence. Disclose both printed problems: reflection-generated dihedral Cayley graphs are bipartite with degree smaller than either part, so diameter two is impossible; and the unspecified reflection set breaks the printed equivalence (classical Singer difference sets give diameter-three graphs for Desarguesian planes). Credit the reduction to Kantor plus Thas-Zagier.

Declare every imported premise: Kantor 1987 (relies on the classification of finite simple groups), the Thas-Zagier special-prime reduction and base-two condition, Feit 8|n, and the derivation of n congruent to 2 modulo 3.
Before the main scan, add the proper-divisor guard q

Cross-checks at main-range modulus sizes must compare full 2^(n+1) mod p residues and actual sieve divisors, not only survivor flags. Any contiguous hash must include every n decision and residue. A uniform failing big-integer bug must not masquerade as no survivors.

A probable-prime test cannot eliminate a survivor. Each survivor needs an exact elimination reason, such as an explicit proper factor or a proved necessary-condition failure; otherwise list it as unresolved.
Cap the main production scan at about 2.5 hours. Report N only as the end of the last unbroken audited block.

Defensible success wording: Assuming the declared imported theorems, one production computation excluded all candidates for 200000000000<=n<N in the audited congruence class; independent arbitrary-precision checks covered only stated subsets. Therefore no non-Desarguesian flag-transitive plane of order less than N exists, conditional on those premises. Never say the extended range was independently certified, and keep the all-orders conjecture open.

Recovered compressed production logs are under selection-inputs/first-attempt-logs/ and must be reconstructed and hash-checked against its manifest without importing producer code. The previous referee result is unverified: logs were absent; sieved-plus-tested counts are not decision audits; Python/C comparison must cross-check arithmetic, not only aggregate counts. Every replay command must finish under 900 seconds.
owner_selection.solved_means: A proof for every order n>8 that no non-Desarguesian finite flag-transitive projective plane exists (equivalently, no special prime p=n^2+n+1), or an explicit counterexample plane verified directly.
owner_selection.partial_means: An exactly scoped verified result, such as a gap-free finite range 200000000000<=n<N with every survivor eliminated under declared imported premises, or a proved new necessary condition.
shared_scope_rules: No automatic revisit, refill, extra problem, paid-API fallback, model/config change, scheduler, commit, push, or external contact.

Sampling is not independent exhaustive verification. Numerical negativity is not a theorem without its analytic bridge. Solver UNKNOWN is not UNSAT.
Openness and novelty are dated search verdicts. Preprints and openai/math are claims until independently established.
shared_review_overrides: This manifest and parent restrictions override stronger promises, confidence labels, and schedules in the screening catalogs.

The sieved+tested=count identity holds by construction in scan.c, so it checks nothing. questions.formal_statement: Does every finite flag-transitive projective plane have to be Desarguesian? Equivalently, for n>8 with p=n^2+n+1 prime, show D={x in F_p*: x^(n+1)=1} is not a planar difference set.
questions.relation_to_book: The geometric nonexistence conjecture is explicitly stated in the article. Its literal diameter-two Cayley-graph assertion is inconsistent; disclose it rather than silently correcting it.
questions.solved_means: A proof for every order n>8 that no non-Desarguesian finite flag-transitive projective plane exists (equivalently, no special prime p=n^2+n+1), or an explicit counterexample plane verified directly.

identified_counterpart.formal_statement: Setting printed in the article: n > 8 is an integer such that p = n² + n + 1 is prime. [ASSUMPTION: standard definitions supplied] A projective plane of order n has n²+n+1 points and n²+n+1 lines. Each line is incident with n+1 points and each point with n+1 lines. Any two distinct points lie on exactly one common line, and any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point. The plane is Desarguesian if it is isomorphic to PG(2,q) over a finite field F_q (then n = q). It is flag-transitive if some group of collineations is transitive on its flags (incident point–line pairs). Conjecture (the article says 'its non-existence is a famous conjecture in geometry'): for no such n does a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n exist. Citing [2]–[4], the article links this to the non-existence of a diameter-3 graph Cay(p); as printed, that Cayley-graph wording is defective (see q4). [ASSUMPTION — supplied general form, using Kantor [3] as cited: a non-Desarguesian flag-transitive plane of order n forces p = n²+n+1 to be prime and a Frobenius group of order p(n+1) to act sharply flag-transitively. Every projective plane of order ≤ 8 is Desarguesian, so the printed conjecture is equivalent to 'every finite flag-transitive projective plane is Desarguesian'.] [ASSUMPTION — supplied number-theoretic form, NOT printed in the article: equivalently, for every n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime, the subgroup D = {x ∈ F_p^* : x^{n+1} = 1} (|D| = n+1) is not a planar (p, n+1, 1) difference set in (Z_p, +). That is, the n(n+1) = p − 1 differences d − d′ (d ≠ d′ in D) do not cover all nonzero residues mod p. For n = 2 and n = 8 this D is a planar difference set, giving PG(2,2) and PG(2,8); this fits the article's restriction n > 8.]
identified_counterpart.solved_means: Either a proof that for every n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime there is no non-Desarguesian flag-transitive projective plane of order n, or a counterexample. By the supplied reformulations, a proof is the same as showing that every finite flag-transitive projective plane is Desarguesian, or that μ_{n+1} ⊂ F_p^* is never a planar difference set mod p for such n. A counterexample would be an explicit non-Desarguesian flag-transitive plane, e.g. an n > 8 with p = n²+n+1 prime for which μ_{n+1} is a planar difference set mod p. Ruling out ranges or congruence classes of n is only partial progress.

sources.finding: Theorem A leaves, besides the classical alternative, a Frobenius group of odd order (n²+n+1)(n+1), with n²+n+1 prime. This supplies the group-theoretic reduction and forces n even, but does not eliminate that alternative. Its proof uses the classification of finite simple groups.

sources.citation: Walter Feit, [Finite projective planes and a question about primes](https://paperzz.com/doc/9103748/finite-projective-planes-and-a-question-about-primes), Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 108 (1990), 561–564; primary article read through a full-text transcription.
sources.finding: Lemma 2.1 supplies d^(n+1)≡1 mod p for every positive divisor d of a putative nonclassical plane order n; Lemma 2.2 supplies 8|n. Taking d=n and using ord_p(n)=3 gives n≡2 mod 3. The additional power-of-two exclusion in Theorem A has a defective argument, identified by later literature, and is not imported here.

sources.citation: Cai Heng Li, [Finite s-arc transitive Cayley graphs and flag-transitive projective planes](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228757029_Finite_s-arc_transitive_Cayley_graphs_and_flag-transitive_projective_planes), Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 133 (2005), 31–41, DOI 10.1090/S0002-9939-04-07549-5.
sources.finding: Example 4.5 supplies Cayley realizations of classical projective-plane incidence graphs using Singer groups and a duality. At n=17, p=307, this gives an admissible reflection-generated dihedral Cayley graph of degree 18 and diameter 3: a counterexample to literal q4. The paper's separate Γ(q) construction specifies an automorphism orbit; it does not justify the book's arbitrary-S equivalence or diameter-two assertion. The valid q3 reduction used here comes from Kantor plus Thas–Zagier.

sources.citation: Binzhou Xia, [Cyclotomic difference sets in finite fields](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1501.03275), Mathematics of Computation 87 (2018), 2461–2482, DOI 10.1090/mcom/3311.
sources.finding: Develops character-sum and polynomial criteria for cyclotomic and modified cyclotomic difference sets, including nonexistence for even indices through 22 other than 2,4,8. Section 5.3 explicitly connects planar difference sets to q3 and retains the conjecture. Its characteristic-two classification does not settle q3, whose ambient field F_p has odd prime order.

sources.citation: Koji Momihara, Qi Wang and Qing Xiang, [Cyclotomy, difference sets, sequences with low correlation, strongly regular graphs, and related geometric substructures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1809.03007), in Combinatorics and Finite Fields (2019), 173–198.
sources.finding: The survey's Section 2.1 and Theorem 2.6 connect q3 to the broader cyclotomic difference-set classification conjectures. It retains these conjectures and discusses the computational exclusion. It also warns that Feit's power-of-two exclusion and Ott's prime-power-order argument contain errors; their combination is not an accepted solution.

sources.citation: Pingzhi Yuan and Hu Yahui, [A note on power residue difference sets](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/256735294_A_note_on_power_residue_difference_sets), Journal of Algebra 291 (2005), 269–273, DOI 10.1016/j.jalgebra.2004.09.029.
